summary: This document described a trivial convention for using HTTP to resolve Uniform Resource Names, as a mechanism the URN working group was considering alongside NAPTR. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Using ordinary web requests to look up where a permanent name currently lives.

subtitle: Using HTTP GET requests to locate resources identified by persistent names.

tldr.problem: URNs are persistent names for resources, but systems need a way to resolve a URN to find the resource or its current location. Existing resolution protocols are complex.
tldr.mechanism: THTTP (Trivial HTTP) encodes URN resolution service requests as HTTP GET requests in a simple format, allowing existing HTTP servers to add resolution support through simple CGI scripts.
tldr.outcome: HTTP servers can serve as URN resolvers without implementing new protocols. However, URN adoption was limited, and this protocol is historic; it represents an experimental approach that did not see widespread deployment.

facts.label: Primary goal
facts.value: Enable existing HTTP servers to resolve URNs

today: RFC 2169 is historic. While THTTP was a simple approach to URN resolution, URNs themselves did not achieve widespread adoption, and this experimental protocol was not standardized. It represents an early attempt to solve the URN resolution problem using familiar HTTP technology.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A Uniform Resource Name (URN) is a permanent, location-independent identifier for a network resource. Unlike a URL, which specifies where a resource is located, a URN identifies what a resource is. For example, a URN might identify a book by its ISBN number, and the resolution process finds where that book is currently available.

The URN Working Group was developing mechanisms to resolve URNs to their current locations or other information. This document describes THTTP (Trivial HTTP), a protocol that leverages existing HTTP servers to provide URN resolution services. Instead of building new server infrastructure, THTTP allows HTTP servers to answer resolution requests using CGI scripts or native HTTP extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: A URN is like "Find the book by J.K. Rowling with ISBN 978-0439-13959-1." A resolver looks that up and tells you where you can currently find that book. THTTP does this lookup using a regular web server.

sections.title: The THTTP Approach
sections.content:
THTTP uses a simple convention to encode URN resolution requests as HTTP GET requests. A client requests a resolution service by sending a GET request to a path containing the service name and the identifier. The path format is /uri-res/ followed by the service name, then a question mark, then the URN or URL being queried.

For example, to resolve a URN to a URL using the N2L (Name to Location) service, a client would send:

GET /uri-res/N2L?urn:foo:12345-54321 HTTP/1.0

The HTTP server handles the request using standard HTTP status codes and response mechanisms. A successful resolution returns 200 (OK) with the resource or a 30X redirect status. A failed resolution returns 404 (Not Found). Access control is handled using standard HTTP status codes like 401 (Unauthorized) or 403 (Forbidden).
sections.plainLanguage: You ask the web server by typing a special web address like "Tell me the location of this permanent name." The server answers with a regular web response, just like any other web request.

sections.title: Resolution Services
sections.content:
THTTP defines several resolution services based on the URN specification. The N2L (URN to Location) service maps a URN to a URL, returned as a Location header with a 30X redirect status. The N2Ls (URN to Locations) service returns a list of URLs as a text/uri-list document.

The N2R (URN to Resource) service returns the actual resource identified by a URN. The N2Rs service returns multiple versions of a resource as a MIME multipart/alternative message. The N2C (URN to URC) service returns a description of the resource, such as a bibliographic citation or metadata.

Additional services include N2Ns (URN to alternative URNs), L2Ns (URL to URNs), L2Ls (URL to alternative URLs), and L2C (URL to URC). The resolver communicates the format of responses using standard HTTP Content-Type headers, and clients can negotiate preferred formats using HTTP Accept headers.
sections.plainLanguage: Different services answer different questions: "Where is this thing?" (N2L), "What is this thing?" (N2R), "What does this thing look like?" (N2C). The server uses regular web mechanisms to send different types of answers.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
THTTP is designed for simplicity of implementation. A resolver can be implemented as a CGI script that reads the request URI from the QUERY_STRING environment variable, performs a database lookup, and returns the appropriate response. The script can look up the URN in a DBM database or any other backing store.

One important requirement is that resolvers must return identical results for lexically equivalent URNs. For example, "urn:cid:foo@huh.com" and "URN:CID:foo@huh.com" must resolve identically, even though they differ in case. Implementations must normalize URNs to a canonical form before database lookups.

Access control can be applied to limit which clients can request which resolution services. The resolver can check the source IP address or require authentication headers. The text/uri-list media type format is defined to support machine-processing of URI lists returned by N2Ls, N2Ns, and similar services.
sections.plainLanguage: You can add URN resolution to a regular web server by writing a simple script that looks things up in a database and gives the answer back as a web page.
